newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan mulls greater consumer financial protection.
newsitem.headline: Japan mulls greater consumer financial protection.

text.p: Japan's planned "Big Bang" deregulation will free up the country's bureaucratic financial industry, but may also initially make it more dangerous for novice investors, government and industry officials say.

"With the Big Bang reforms, it is likely that more individual investors, who don't know much about financial markets, will participate in the market," an official at the Ministry of Finance's (MOF) finance company division said.

The ministry, joined by the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI), has started discussing the possibility of drafting new consumer protection laws by consolidating current rules, which cover one sector, such as banks, but not other sectors such as non-bank financial institutions.

"Consumer protection laws have been implemented in Europe and the United States and we need to catch up with international standards," said Hiroshi Suzuki, senior deputy director of MITI's commercial and consumer credit division.
Consumer protection measures for both individual investors and borrowers will be included in the detailed Big Bang proposals due out in June, the Finance Ministry official said.
Monetary authorities say they have been alarmed by small investors' purchases of high-risk investments, but there is no administrative framework to protect them from taking excessive risks.

In the past few years, private investors in Japan have bought foreign bonds and dual-currency bonds, ignoring possible currency risks, because of the higher returns on those bonds compared with domestic bonds which offer lower yields.
Japan's interest rates are currently at rock-bottom levels.
A record 2.4 trillion yen ($19.0 billion) worth of dual-currency bonds was issued in 1996, underwriting sources said.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of MOF's International Finance Bureau, told Reuters recently that brokerage houses which sell foreign bonds and dual-currency bonds should properly explain the inherent dangers in investing in them.
The Big Bang deregulation could also lead to a widening gap between individuals and financial institutions in acquiring information on financial markets, ministry officials said.

Once the Big Bang reforms get under way, individuals must deal more carefully with financial institutions, said the Finance Ministry official, adding administrative measures would be needed to protect consumers.
Ministry officials also said there have been cases of private information on individual borrowers being used to identify targets for future loans.
Under current rules there are no penalties for doing that.
A new MOF-MITI committee aims to propose measures to protect consumers by safeguarding their credit information, they said.

"Some may say individuals should be responsible for themselves, but we think financial institutions should be careful in handling personal credit information," said Kousuke Imashimizu, director of MITI's commercial and consumer credit division.

He said better control of consumers' credit information may help reduce the number of personal bankruptcies in Japan, which jumped to about 56,500 cases in 1996, compared with 43,400 cases in 1995. ($1=126 yen)
